title: What to watch: targets, doubles and the pre-shot routine
summary: Learn to notice the target type, its flight line, the kind of double and the shooter's routine in Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting, so that the shots stop looking alike.

body.html: At first, all shots look alike: a target flies, a bang, pieces. An experienced spectator sees much more. In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting each target is a small puzzle, and it is interesting to watch how the shooter solves it.

Start with the type of target. The most common one is the standard target. The midi and the mini are smaller and look further away than they are. A battue is thin and flat and flies edge-on. A rabbit rolls and bounces along the ground. Sizes and other types: Types of clay targets.

Next, the trajectory, the path the target follows. It may come towards the shooter (incomer), fly away (going away), cross in front (crosser), spring almost straight up (teal) or fly a wide arc (looper). Try to name the trajectory before the shot. The Practice game “Name the flight” trains exactly this.
Left and right are usually given from the shooter's side. If you stand facing the shooter, their “left to right” is your right to left.

Doubles are two targets for one call: the shooter calls once and shoots at both. Watch them separately. In a double on report the second target is launched when the shooter fires at the first. In a simultaneous double both targets fly out at the same moment. In a rafale two targets leave the same trap (the machine that throws the targets) one after the other, along the same line. More in Singles and doubles.

html.sporting: Squads of at most six shooters walk from stand to stand across the ground. On each stand they usually shoot the singles first, then the doubles: on report, simultaneous or rafale. The stock is the part of the gun that goes to the shoulder. Until the target appears, its top must stay below the line on the vest, drawn 25 cm below the shoulder axis (an imaginary line through both shoulders). So you see the whole gun mount: the gun coming up to the shoulder and cheek.
html.compak: A squad of at most six shooters shoots from five stations in a line, at targets from six traps (the machines that throw the targets). The shooters take turns, five targets each; when the shooter on station 5 has finished, everyone moves one station to the right. Doubles are on report or simultaneous. When a Compak® Sporting shooter calls for the target, the gun may already be at the shoulder or still lowered: the rules leave this free. So some shooters call with the gun already “mounted”, that is, at the shoulder.

body.html: Then watch the shooter's pre-shot routine: the same steps in the same order before each target. Many shooters point their feet towards the break point, the spot where they plan to break the target. Then they point the muzzles (the front ends of the barrels) at the hold point, where the gun waits for the target. Next they put their eyes on the pick-up point, where the target is first seen clearly. Only then do they call for the target: a short word, such as “pull”, and the target is launched. The seconds may vary a little; the order stays the same.

Listen to the referee as well. Only the referee decides whether a target is hit or lost (zero). In Compak® Sporting the rules ask the referee to announce each zero aloud or with a sound signal. Count the score along with the referee, but keep your opinion of a call to yourself. How to behave near the stand: A spectator at the ground: where to stand, how to photograph and support.

key_points.html: Tell the targets apart: standard, midi, mini, battue, rabbit.
Try to name the trajectory before the shot.
Doubles on report and simultaneous doubles exist in both disciplines; the rafale only in Sporting™.
A good routine is the same steps in the same order.
Only the referee decides: count along, but do not comment on a call.

did_you_know.html: For part of its flight a battue shows only its edge, a thin line that is hard to see. Then it tilts, shows its flat face and drops fast. Watch how shooters choose the moment to fire.

quiz.q: Which target rolls and bounces along the ground?
quiz.explain: A rabbit is a thick, strong target rolled on its edge along the ground.

quiz.q: Which kind of double exists only in Sporting™?
quiz.explain: A Compak® Sporting double is on report or simultaneous; the rafale belongs to Sporting™ only.

quiz.q: What should stay the same in a good pre-shot routine?
quiz.explain: Many coaches suggest the same steps in the same order; the time may vary a little within the time limit.
